title: Amitabh Bachchan and Amish Tripathi Are Building India's First AAA Video Game — and It's Based on the Ramayan
excerpt: The Age of Bhaarat pairs India's biggest literary mythologist with its most iconic actor for a console-and-PC game that aims to compete with God of War and Assassin's Creed.
body:
In a revelation that has sent the Indian gaming community into overdrive, bestselling author **Amish Tripathi** has confirmed that he's building a AAA video game based on the Ramayan — and **Amitabh Bachchan** is attached.

The project, titled **'The Age of Bhaarat'**, was revealed during a preview segment of *Cyrus Says*, where Amish described it as "the game India has been waiting to make for twenty years." The collaboration pairs India's biggest literary mythologist with its most iconic living actor, and the ambition is unmistakable: this isn't a mobile game with microtransactions. It's a full-scale, console-and-PC release targeting global audiences.

## What We Know

Details remain carefully guarded, but here's what Amish has shared:

- **Studio:** The game is being developed by **Tara Gaming**, a new Indian studio backed by a mix of domestic and international investors
- **Genre:** An open-world action-RPG set in the world of the Ramayan, drawing from Amish's own *Ram Chandra* series (which reimagined the epic as grounded historical fiction)
- **Amitabh's role:** Bachchan will provide voice, motion capture, and likeness for a central character — widely speculated to be Rishi Vishwamitra, the sage who trains the young Ram
- **Scale:** AAA production values — meaning budgets, team size, and visual fidelity comparable to titles like *God of War* or *Assassin's Creed*

## Why This Matters

India consumes an enormous amount of games — the country has over **520 million gamers** as of 2025, making it one of the world's largest gaming populations. But the vast majority play free-to-play mobile titles like BGMI and Free Fire. India has never produced a console-quality AAA game that competed on the global stage.

The closest precedent is **Raji: An Ancient Epic** (2020), an indie action-adventure set in Hindu mythology that won critical acclaim and sold well internationally, proving there's a global appetite for Indian mythological settings. The Age of Bhaarat appears to be attempting that same cultural proposition, but at a scale fifty times larger.

For NRIs in the gaming community — and there are millions of them, from teenage gamers in New Jersey to game developers at studios like Riot, Ubisoft, and EA — this is a long-awaited moment. Indian mythology has been the source material for countless Western games (Asura's Wrath, Smite, various Unreal Engine demos), but always filtered through Western studios. The Age of Bhaarat would be the first time an Indian story of this scale is told by Indians, for a global audience.

## The Bachchan Factor

Amitabh Bachchan's involvement is more than a marketing play. At 83, Bachchan remains India's most recognisable voice — literally. His narration carries an authority and gravitas that no other Indian actor can match. If The Age of Bhaarat's storytelling leans on Amish's literary style (gritty, humanised mythology with moral ambiguity), Bachchan's voice could ground the game the way Keanu Reeves grounded *Cyberpunk 2077*.

Amish Tripathi, meanwhile, brings a track record of making ancient mythology feel urgent and modern. His *Shiva Trilogy* has sold over 8 million copies. His *Ram Chandra* series reimagined Sita as a warrior-diplomat. If anyone can write a game narrative that doesn't treat the Ramayan as sacred museum piece but as a living, playable story, it's him.

## When Can We Play It?

No release date has been announced. Given the realities of AAA game development — even established studios take 4-6 years — The Age of Bhaarat is likely years away from launch. But the fact that it exists, with this pedigree, is already a statement.

**For NRI gamers:** Keep an eye on Tara Gaming's social channels. If this project delivers even half its promise, it could do for Indian gaming what *RRR* did for Telugu cinema — prove that the talent, the stories, and the ambition were always there. They just needed someone to go big.
